(a) The violation starts in the gold, ChartFactory.putItemValue. The fault is that `if (order > 0) break;` has lost its `ascending &&` guard. So on an unsorted list the walk stops at the first greater item and inserts a second item with x = 3.0, and the existing item never gets the new y-value. The other hops only pass values on or count items. Their "adds or updates" wording fails only because the gold fails underneath them.

(b) Every hop's javadoc matches its code.

(c) None of the three declared hop edits absorbs the fault. A hop cannot fix it by preparing the list beforehand or tidying it afterwards without reordering the series, because the gold's own walk never reaches the existing item. The only edit that passes everything is a bypass in hop 1 (CategoryPlot.storeXYValue): look the item up with series.indexOf, then updateByIndex. It passes the trigger, the ownership tests and the full suite.

(d) The names are neutral and there is no fault vocabulary. The lie says the new y-value is written to a copy of the list and the copy then replaces it. It names neither the fault nor the omitted step.

(e) The five hosts match the seeded 1500-regime draw for seed 6087, with XYSeries.java excluded: CategoryPlot, Axis, AbstractRenderer, DateAxis, ChartFactory. The gold is five calls below the facade. The facade is a guard plus state gathering plus one call, passing `this` and its fields (variants V1 and V2). The trigger is an existing test and test.patch is empty.

(f) XYSeries.indexOf pins the convention outside the gold. Its javadoc says an unsorted series is searched by iterating through all items, and update, remove(Number) and add(XYDataItem, boolean) use it in production. testIndexOf2 and testUpdate2 pass on that path.

(g) The C10i rules hold. No existing visibility is widened: hop 1 uses only the public XYSeries.add and Series.fireSeriesChanged. There is no new type and no reflection. The facade's signature, modifiers and thrown types are unchanged, and no test is edited.

One note for the trace checker, not an ownership problem: in the gold, the match test depends on `ascending` but the early break below it does not. The gold's javadoc also ties "inserted at its place in that order" to ascending lists only.

T1.why: Every parameter feeds the main computation: items is searched and inserted into, x and y build entry and are used in equals and setY, and ascending chooses the match test in the ternary.

T2.why: position goes up by one each iteration and sets where the item is inserted, entry is compared and added, order drives both the match and the break, previous is returned; neither ternary branch can be removed without changing behaviour, and the break decision is live.

T3.why: I am unsure, so I count it as a trace: the loop makes two parallel decisions, and the ascending flag (whose javadoc limits ordered insertion to "a list held in ascending order") splits the match decision into ascending and non-ascending cases but not the break-and-insert decision, which applies the ascending-order break even when ascending is false.

T4.why: The concrete claims are met: the @return copy (previous) and the null return on add both happen, ordered insertion for ascending lists is done by the order > 0 break, and "null not permitted" on items and x is a caller precondition.

build.reason:
Both allowed facades are reached by existing tests, but neither can carry a quiet one-line omission that exactly one existing test catches. That is the single-trigger rule (gate G5); the other option would be adding computation the facade does not have.

1. POJONode.toString
- The only test that reaches it is TestJsonNode::testPOJO (full-suite probe), and its only call checks new POJONode("x").toString() == "x".
- The value "x" takes the default path, `String.valueOf(_value)`: one library call with no decision or loop.
- The byte[] and RawValue special cases are never reached by any test.
- So no omission in any behaviour-preserving split of toString can change the result for "x". The only way would be to remove the result itself, which leaves a visibly broken idiom.

2. POJONode.serialize
- The computation is a three-way dispatch: null -> ctxt.defaultSerializeNull(gen); JsonSerializable -> its own serialize(gen, ctxt); otherwise -> ctxt.defaultSerializeValue(_value, gen).
- The first two branches are subsumed by the third. SerializerProvider.defaultSerializeValue already writes null exactly as defaultSerializeNull does, and it routes a JsonSerializable through SerializableSerializer to value.serialize(gen, provider).
- Measured with full-suite runs on scratch copies:
  - JsonSerializable branch dropped: 0 failing tests.
  - null branch dropped: 0 failing tests.
  - default call dropped: 4 failing tests (testPOJONodeCustomSer, testPOJOIntArray, testPOJOString, testPOJOBean), and the gold writes nothing for ordinary values.
- The 7 reaching tests fall into three groups: {Data with a custom serializer that reads a provider attribute}, {three RawValue tests}, {int[], String, Bean}. The facade's computation has no step that tells testPOJONodeCustomSer, the real bug's test, apart from the other non-JsonSerializable values. Only the provider attribute or the generator-versus-context route does, and neither is a decision the facade makes.
- Isolating one test would need invented steps that are not part of the facade, such as copying RawValue's private raw-writing logic or a serializer lookup by value kind. The addendum forbids this ("never copy private logic into a hop"; the chain only redistributes the facade's computation).

Neither allowed candidate can carry the recipe validly, so the instance is UNBUILDABLE. No design, spec or instance files were written.

build.reason:
The trigger rule cannot be met: any omission must be caught by exactly one existing test, and none is. I ran the full suite with logging in LookupTranslator.translate (424k calls: table shortest/longest, input length, index, clamped window, matched length, replacement type and length). The method's steps that change behaviour, and how many of the 26 reaching tests each one affects:
- **End-of-input clamp:** used by 11 tests. Dropping it throws in all 11. Replacing it with an early `return 0` fails 6: testUnescapeJava, testStandaloneAmphersand, testUnescapeHtml4, testLang313, testEscapeHtmlVersions, testEscapeXml.
- **Matches below the full window** (the shortening descent): 3 tests (testEscapeXml, testStandaloneAmphersand, testUnescapeHtml4).
- **Greedy longest-first order:** no test sees it. Turning the loop into an ascending one gave 0 failing tests. The only prefix keys are in UNESCAPE_JAVA, and its tested inputs give the same result either way.
- **Converting the window to a String key** (the LANG-882 convention): no test sees it. Removing `.toString()` gave 0 failing tests, because String.subSequence and StringBuffer.subSequence both return a String.
- **Writing the replacement and returning the consumed count:** used by every test.

The only behaviours that a single test exercises are data properties of one table entry:
- the empty replacement of UNESCAPE_JAVA's lone backslash (testUnescapeJava);
- a StringBuffer replacement (testLang882);
- one intermediate-length unclamped match, "&" followed by text (testUnescapeHtml4).

No ordinary step of a lookup routine handles one of these differently, so no one-line omission could target it. Options I considered and rejected:
- A char-by-char write or a found-flag/buffer formulation built to break only on an empty replacement.
- A String cast or instanceof branch that breaks only on a StringBuffer value.
- A "try the full window, then the shortest" descent that misses only the intermediate match.

Each of these would be a construction no natural lookup routine has, a modification rather than an omission, or a visible local trace (T2 frozen or dead local, T3 or T4). Shaping traffic with shortcuts in hops 1-4 (single-length tables, fewer characters left than the shortest key, a first-character prefix filter) still leaves at least 3 tests on every candidate step. The allowed list holds only this method, so no other facade could be used.

build.gold: org.apache.commons.math3.linear.BlockRealMatrix::decadeOf(int limb) (hop 5). It returns the decimal exponent of a base-10000 limb, documented as the exponent of the greatest power of ten below the limb, or zero for a limb of at most one. It first estimates the value from the binary length, `(31 - Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(FastMath.max(limb, 1))) * 1233 >> 12`, then refines it once against `FastMath.pow(10, decade + 1)`. A brute-force check over all limbs 0..9999 shows the correct chain equals the original threshold cascade on every limb, including the strict-comparison behaviour at 10, 100 and 1000.

build.fault: A one-line omission of the refinement step in the gold: `return limb > FastMath.pow(10, decade + 1) ? decade + 1 : decade;` becomes `return decade;`. DfpDec.nextAfter reaches log10 only with the limbs 0, 1, 999 and 9999, where the estimate is exact. Dfp.toDouble only searches upwards from its starting estimate, so a lower log10 changes none of its results. That makes testLog10 the only test that newly fails.

No allowed facade can carry a valid C10i design.

1. hashCode() returns getName().hashCode(). Any chain computes a deterministic function of the name, so every map lookup through it stays correct whatever omission the gold has. No test asserts a hash value. So no omission has an existing trigger.

2. getExtraField(ZipShort) is the lookup behind every Zip64 and Unicode extra-field access in ZipFile, ZipArchiveInputStream, ZipArchiveOutputStream and ZipUtil (91 tests reach it directly). Any omission in the per-field match changes the lookup for dozens of tests, which breaks gate G5. The finer behaviours (duplicate header ids, first vs last match) are never tested.

3. setUnixMode(int) computes four things:
   - the mode in the upper 16 bits;
   - the MS-DOS read-only bit, set when owner write 0200 is absent;
   - the 0x10 directory flag;
   - platform = PLATFORM_UNIX.

   Two of these are pinned: the mode placement (by getUnixMode and the ZipFile round trip) and the platform (by getPlatform's javadoc). But omitting either fails two tests, testUnixMode and ZipTestCase::testUnixModeInAddRaw, verified on the full suite.

   The two MS-DOS bits are single-trigger: omitting either fails only testUnixMode. But the low-byte MS-DOS convention appears in no other production code. The only mentions are setUnixMode's own inline comments, which go away when the body is replaced. There is no sibling, no reader of DOS attributes, and no Info-ZIP or MS-DOS mapping elsewhere: AsiExtraField maps Unix type bits, and SevenZ attributes are only stored. No passing test checks the low two bytes either.

   So the External pins rule cannot be met. BUILD_BRIEF lists it as a validity rule, and the auditor's item (f) requires it for CONFIRMED. A further problem: dropping the directory flag under V1 would leave the gold's directory parameter unused, which is a T1 trace.

The only remaining single-trigger fault would therefore be an unpinned convention, which the brief says not to force.

audit.summary:
CONFIRMED. Audit file: /Users/shawnli/Desktop/Honours/defects4j/.claude/worktrees/strict-depth-experiment-run-524113/supervisor_pipeline_runs/weaker-model-v1/construction/mainrun/audits/MI-Compress-13.json.

I reproduced the instance. The variant compiles. The trigger ZipArchiveEntryTest::testUnixMode fails with expected:<16> but was:<0>. Both ownership tests pass, and the full suite has only the trigger failing.

(a) TarArchiveEntry.putUnixMode is the only method that builds the attribute word. Its javadoc promises "the form used for entries made on a Unix system". It sets the read-only bit but leaves out the 0x10 directory bit. Hops 1-4 pass the entry and mode down unchanged.

(b) The hop javadocs are generic delegation statements and match their code.

(c) No edit to the arguments at any hop can produce 0x10. Adding the flag after the gold returns, in the facade or in hop 4, passes every test, but it overwrites the gold's result, so it is a bypass.

(d) The names are neutral, and the facade's added false sentence (about masking modes above 07777) does not mention the directory flag.

(e) The gold is five calls below the facade. The hosts are exactly the five largest5 hosts in hop order. The facade is the allowed setUnixMode, passing `this` (variant V2) with one delegating call.

(f) AsiExtraField (testModes) and isDirectory (testExplicitDirectoryEntry) pin the convention that the stored Unix data records a directory. The exact 0x10 value comes from the MS-DOS/Info-ZIP standard, which the javadocs refer to.

(g) Nothing is widened, no type is added, there is no reflection, the facade's signature is unchanged and no test is edited.

T1.why: Both parameters feed the side effect: `entry` receives the setExternalAttributes call and `mode` is shifted and masked into its argument.

T2.why: The method has no locals, and the only decision, `(mode & 0200) == 0 ? 1 : 0`, gives different values that change the stored attributes, so it is not a dead decision.

T3.why: Only one low-order attribute bit is derived (read-only from owner-write 0200), the gold's text names no closed set of attribute bits or flags, and no handled sibling has an untreated partner, so this is at most one member of a larger unnamed set.

T4.why: The javadoc's "Stores a Unix mode in the external attributes ... in the form used for entries made on a Unix system" is a general description of the encoding that the body does address (mode << 16 into setExternalAttributes); it names no concrete limit, value class or case that the body visibly fails to meet.

(b) Each hop's javadoc matches its code. Hops 2 and 4 are loosely documented but only delegate.
(c) No competing repair found. Two caller-side pre-filters pass the trigger, the ownership tests and the full suite: nulling the unflagged timestamps at the facade, or at hop 1. I recorded both as bypasses because putTimes still contradicts its own javadoc after either edit. The hop-3 trim-by-bitCount edit fails testSampleFile.
(d) Names are neutral and the lie names neither the omitted check nor any hop.
(e) Hosts match hosts_hop_order exactly; the gold is five calls below the facade (V1 state gathering plus one call). Only the trigger newly fails.

(g) The facade's signature, modifiers and @Override are unchanged; no visibility is widened, no type added, no reflection used, no test edited.
Reviewer concern: the build brief requires a fault that no caller can pre-filter. Here the facade can pre-filter it, which is what the original method did.

T1.why: flags feeds head, which is written to buffer[0]; stamps decides the null test and the putLong writes; buffer receives every write; so each parameter's value affects a side effect or the return value.

T2.why: head is masked, cleared in the loop and written to buffer[0]; count is initialised to 1, used as the putLong write position, advanced by 4 in the loop and returned; bit feeds head's update; i advances; and both branches of the null test have different live effects, so there is no dead or frozen local and no dead decision.

T3.why: The loop covers every index of stamps, both the null and non-null cases get distinct treatment, and the gold names no closed set (enum, type code or two-member pair) of which some member is left out.

T4.why: Each concrete javadoc claim is met by a line of the body: flags are restricted to the timestamp bits (flags & ((1 << stamps.length) - 1)), the bit of a missing stamp is cleared (head &= ~bit), each written stamp takes the next four bytes (putLong at count; count += 4), and the byte count is returned. The buffer-room clause is a caller precondition. No phrase in the text says that only timestamps whose bit is set are written, so any concern about a flags/data mismatch would come from outside knowledge of the format, not from the text.

- Hop 1 forms the shape a = x + 1.
- Hop 2 makes Gamma's regime decision: below a + 1 it returns 1 - P(a, x) from Gamma's series (Gamma.regularizedGammaP); otherwise it calls hop 3.
- Hop 3 divides exp(-x + a log x - logGamma(a)) by the value of the fraction.
- Hop 4 passes the arguments on.
- The gold evaluates the continued fraction.

Why this test and this fault: seven tests reach the facade. I instrumented Gamma and ContinuedFraction on those tests, and the instrumentation showed that only testCumulativeProbabilitySpecial and testLargeMeanInverseCumulativeProbability ever need the fraction rescaled. The large-mean inverse test can only fail on NaN or an exception, because its assertions are the bisection's own invariant. The gold returns the last finite convergent when the next one is NaN, so in the variant that test passes and only the trigger fails.

- Evidence: ContinuedFraction::evaluate, whose javadoc says the intermediate results "are scaled whenever they threaten to become numerically unstable"; Gamma::regularizedGammaQ, which uses the same fraction; and Beta::regularizedBeta.
- Ownership tests: ContinuedFractionTest::testGoldenRatio, GammaTest::testRegularizedGammaPositivePositive and PoissonDistributionTest::testCumulativeProbabilities.

Audit written to /Users/shawnli/Desktop/Honours/defects4j/.claude/worktrees/strict-depth-experiment-run-524113/supervisor_pipeline_runs/weaker-model-v1/construction/mainrun/audits/MI-Math-75.json (its d_leakage field is false, the correct value). (c) Competing repair found: the omitted Integer->Long key conversion can be done by any caller first. A one-line conversion in the facade, and another in hop 4, each pass the trigger, the three ownership tests and the full suite (0 failures). Neither replaces the gold's work. Both match the evidence methods getCount and getCumFreq, which do this conversion at their own entry. This also breaks the BUILD_BRIEF rule that no caller can pre-filter the fault. The declared compensating edits leave this conversion out, so G9 never tested it. (d) The d field is wrongly set to true here: no leakage was found and the lie does not name the conversion. (e) Conforms: 5 hops, distinct hosts, seeded draw matches, V1 facade, empty test.patch, only the trigger fails. (f) Pinned by the class javadoc, getCount/getCumFreq, the addValue overloads and the passing ownership tests. C10i rules followed: allowed facade, signature unchanged, nothing widened, no new types, no reflection, no test edits.

T1.why: table, value and occurrences are all read in the main computation (get/put key, and the count stored or added).

T2.why: The only local, count, decides which branch runs and feeds the put in the else branch, and the two branches have different effects, so nothing is dead or frozen and no decision is dead.

T3.why: The only set handled is absent (null) versus present count, and both cases are handled; no closed set of siblings is left partly treated.

T4.why: The javadoc's concrete rule, that a value not yet held is entered with the number of occurrences as its count, is done by table.put(value, Long.valueOf(occurrences)), and the general add-to-count description is done by the else branch.

No allowed facade has a one-line omission that is both caught by exactly one existing test and impossible for a caller to pre-filter or recover. The BUILD_BRIEF fault rule (the step must sit in an iteration or decision no caller can pre-filter or recover) and the single-owner rule (W13) cannot both be met.

(1) addValue(Comparable<?>) does three things:
- An Integer-to-Long key step. Its only trigger is testIntegerValues, but it is a pure function of the single value v that the facade and every hop hold. A one-line conversion anywhere above the gold repairs it, and that matches Frequency's own convention: getCount and getCumFreq convert at their entry. This was v1's rejection, and moving the step to another hop or splitting it differently keeps it pre-filterable.
- A ClassCastException-to-IllegalArgumentException translation (trigger testAdd only, M4). Any caller can recover it with a one-line try/catch. If the gold swallows the exception instead, a caller can still pre-filter it with a one-line table probe, and the empty catch in the variant risks a T2(c) trace.
- The count arithmetic (M3). It is not caller-recoverable, but every omission there fails testCounts, testPcts and testIntegerValues (gate G5), and the method has no iteration or comparator-specific step that only one test covers.

(2) getCount(Comparable<?>): every one-line omission is caught by two or three tests (M1: three; M2: two; the null-to-0 step: many).

(3) addValue(Object): its only step is an instanceof argument check. Its omission (trigger testAddNonComparable, M5) can be pre-filtered by any caller. Moved into the gold it would be an argument check, which the T1 rule treats as a parameter used only for checking.

build.reason:
No single-trigger quiet omission exists for the only allowed facade.

getSlope's whole computation is a scalar quotient sumXY/sumXX of three fields, behind two guards (n<2 and |sumXX| below a tolerance). Any faithful chain only redistributes this, so the omission screen on the original body (7 reaching tests) holds for every hop split:
- M1, dropping the count guard: no test newly fails.
- M2, dropping the variation guard: no test newly fails.
- M3, dropping both: no test newly fails.
The reason is that sumXX and sumXY are exactly 0 whenever n<2 or all x are equal (the only degenerate inputs, all in testNaNs), so 0/0 already yields NaN.

The observable behaviours are caught by more than one test:
- the sign (M4, Math.abs) fails testCorr and testPerfectNegative;
- the magnitude is pinned by testNorris, testInference, testPerfect and testRandom.

The only single-trigger route (M5: omit the variation guard and add a `sumProducts == 0 -> return 0d` fast path, which fails testNaNs alone) is invalid on three counts:
- (a) In the variant gold the zero numerator is handled but the zero denominator is not, which is T3(b), one half of a pair.
- (b) In the correct gold the fast path differs from the fall-through only by the sign of zero, which is a T2(c) dead-decision risk.
- (c) Any hop 1-4 or the facade holds the same three scalars and can pre-filter in one line (`if (Math.abs(sxx) < 10*Double.MIN_VALUE) return Double.NaN;`, which is the original guard). That violates the brief's 'no caller can pre-filter or recover' fault rule and the single-owner rule (G9).

There is no per-element computation to place in the gold, and no other allowed candidate exists. This is the pre-registered batch-8 UNBUILDABLE kind 'no single-trigger omission / nothing to split'.
